content: Elevated cholesterol levels typically do not produce specific symptoms unless they have been present for a prolonged period. However, certain types of hypercholesterolemia can result in distinct physical manifestations. In the head, eyes, ears, nose, and throat (HEENT) examination: Arcus senilis may be observed, which is characterized by a white or grayish discoloration at the periphery of the cornea. Xanthelasma palpebrarum may also be present, appearing as yellowish, lipid-rich deposits or patches around the eyelids. In the cardiovascular and pulmonary systems: Signs of congestive heart failure may be noted, which can include pulmonary rales (crackling sounds heard during auscultation) due to ischemia or myocardial infarction (heart attack). In the extremities: Xanthomas may be identified, which are areas of tendon thickening caused by cholesterol deposition. There may be diminished or absent pulses in the femoral, posterior tibial, and dorsalis pedis arteries, along with the presence of a femoral bruit, which are indicative of peripheral artery disease (PAD). In the neurological examination: There may be evidence of transient ischemic attacks (TIAs) or cerebrovascular accidents (strokes), which are associated with cholesterol-related vascular disease.
